meta.title: Who really said "He Is a Self-Made Man.” “Yes, And He Worships His Creator"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Disraeli was the target, not the speaker. The jibe is Henry Clapp’s, aimed at Horace Greeley in 1868; a 1964 book reversed the roles.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He Is a Self-Made Man.” “Yes, And He Worships His Creator'?
meta.ogDescription: Not said BY Disraeli - said ABOUT him, and first about someone else entirely.

answer.label: Not Disraeli — the jibe is Henry Clapp’s, aimed at Horace Greeley
answer.authorDates: American editor and wit · died 1875 · editor of the New York Saturday Press
answer.sourceLine: Disraeli is on the wrong side of this one. Quote Investigator credits the core of the joke to William Allen Butler’s 1858 poem Two Millions, and the modern wording to Henry Clapp, whose line about Horace Greeley — ‘a self made man, and worships his creator’ — ran in newspapers in March 1868. By June 1870 an English version had John Bright saying of Disraeli that ‘he adores his maker’. Disraeli was the target. He becomes the speaker only in 1964, when a book on political wit reversed the two men.

source.excerpt: Henry Clapp says that Horace Greeley is a self made man, and worships his creator.
trail: Quote Investigator concludes that ‘based on current evidence the core of this joke should be credited to William Allen Butler who wrote the poem “Two Millions” in 1858’, and that the modern version emerged in 1868 with Henry Clapp criticising Horace Greeley: quoteinvestigator.com ↗.
Butler’s poem was written for the Phi Beta Kappa Society of Yale College and delivered on 28 July 1858; Google Books serves the D. Appleton edition in full view: books.google.com ↗.

The Disraeli connection runs the other way. QI quotes a June 1870 item — ‘One of Mr. Disraeli’s admirers, in speaking about him to John Bright, said, “You ought to give him credit for what he has accomplished, as he is a self-made man.” “I know he is,” retorted Mr. Bright, “and he adores his maker.”’ Disraeli is the subject of the insult, not its author.

QI records that The Fine Art of Political Wit (1964) ‘presented a version of the anecdote that flipped two traditional roles’, making Disraeli the speaker and Bright the target — which is the version now in circulation.
source.excerptNote: Butler’s 1858 poem carries the idea without the epigram: a millionaire who kept the higher law ‘To love his maker, for he was SELF-MADE! / Self-made, self-trained, self-willed, self-satisfied’. Quote Investigator notes Butler’s lines were fiction, criticising nobody in particular.

author.name: Henry Clapp
author.heading: About Henry Clapp
author.metaLine: American editor and wit · died 1875 · editor of the New York Saturday Press
author.bio: Henry Clapp Jr. edited The Saturday Press, the New York literary weekly that spotlighted Walt Whitman and first published Mark Twain’s first short story in 1865. This line was the piece of talk that outlived him: a letter of reminiscence printed in the Boston Globe in 1875, the year he died, called it his most brilliant piece of wit and set out the exchange with Greeley that produced it.

copyAttribution: Not said by Disraeli — said about him. The jibe is Henry Clapp’s, aimed at Horace Greeley in March 1868; the core idea is William Allen Butler’s poem "Two Millions" (1858).

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one has been mis-told in an unusual way: not just given to the wrong person, but pointed the wrong direction.

items.why: In the earliest English telling — June 1870 — the line is said about Disraeli by John Bright, in the form ‘he adores his maker’. QI dates the flip that made Disraeli the speaker to a 1964 book: Quote Investigator ↗.
Bright’s version is real but it is neither the first nor this wording: it dates from 1870, two years after Clapp’s, and says ‘adores his maker’: Quote Investigator ↗.

Evan Esar’s 1949 Dictionary of Humorous Quotations attributed it to the poet Cowper, who died in 1800; Quote Investigator calls the ascription anomalous and it was copied into later collections: Quote Investigator ↗.
The New York Tribune editor was the man Clapp was mocking in 1868. Harper’s reported in July that year that nobody laughed harder than Greeley: Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is William Allen Butler’s, from 1858; the epigram is Henry Clapp’s, from 1868, and it was aimed at Horace Greeley: Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a small logical trap. If a man is genuinely self-made, then his creator is himself — so praising him for worshipping his creator convicts him of vanity while appearing to compliment his piety.

It arrived when ‘self-made man’ was becoming the central boast of American public life, which is why it found Horace Greeley first: a printer’s apprentice turned newspaper baron who never stopped mentioning it.
detailsBody: Butler wrote Two Millions for Yale’s Phi Beta Kappa Society in 1858; it was reprinted in London in Titan that November and excerpted by reviewers in The Knickerbocker.

After Clapp, the line was reused freely — Junius Henri Browne applied it to the New York financier George Law in 1869, and Howard Crosby printed it in The Phrenological Journal in 1880 crediting only ‘some wag’.
